concept: Passive-voice template selection by root class (hollow root)
prompt: A learner forms the passive perfect of the hollow root ق و ل by writing قُوِلَ — treating the middle radical و like an ordinary consonant that takes a damma then a kasra, the way a sound root's passive perfect works (كُتِبَ from ك ت ب). What is the actual passive perfect of قَالَ, and why can't the sound-stem template be applied letter-by-consonant here?
expected_answer: The correct passive perfect is قِيلَ: a single long vowel ī replaces the whole perfect-stem vowel melody. The hollow root's middle radical و cannot itself carry a separate damma then kasra the way an ordinary consonant does, so the sound-stem consonant-by-consonant template قُوِلَ is not merely an alternate spelling but a wrong construction; the root's class (sound vs. hollow) must be checked before selecting which passive template applies.
accepted_variants: قِيلَ is correct because a hollow root's medial glide cannot bear its own separate vowel pairing, so the whole stem takes one long vowel instead of the sound-root damma-kasra template.
forbidden_answers: قُوِلَ لأن نفس قاعدة كُتِبَ تُطبّق على كل الأفعال بغض النظر عن نوع الجذر
قِيلَ is correct because the sound-stem consonant-by-consonant passive rule always applies to every Arabic verb regardless of root type.
required_reasoning: the middle radical is a glide that cannot itself carry a separate damma and kasra the way an ordinary consonant does
the hollow-root passive realizes as one long vowel across the stem, not consonant-by-consonant vowels
the root's class (sound vs hollow) must be checked before selecting which passive template applies
explanation: A hollow root's medial glide cannot bear the sound-stem consonant-by-consonant passive vowel pairing; its passive perfect instead realizes as a single long vowel across the whole stem.

concept: Hamza-final noun wrongly assimilated into the manqus (glide-final) class
prompt: قَاضِ (a manqus noun) drops its bare final glide ي in the indefinite nominative and genitive, replacing it with tanwin kasratan alone. A learner reasons that بَرِيءٌ 'innocent' (root ب ر أ, ending in a hamza after a long vowel) must behave the same way, since it 'also ends in a weak-looking letter,' and writes its indefinite genitive as بَرِيِ (hamza dropped, bare tanwin kasratan). Is this correct? Justify from the noun's final-letter class.
expected_answer: This is wrong. بَرِيءٌ is a hamza-final noun, not a manqus (bare-glide-final) noun; its final hamza is a full consonant that carries its own case vowel and tanwin directly and visibly in every case, so the indefinite genitive is بَرِيءٍ (hamza visible, kasratan on the hamza), never بَرِيِ. The manqus hidden-exponent rule (glide drop plus bare tanwin) applies only to a noun whose bare final radical is a single glide preceded by kasra, and a hamza-final noun does not qualify for that class merely because it looks similarly irregular.
accepted_variants: بَرِيءٍ keeps its hamza with its own visible kasratan in the indefinite genitive, because a hamza-final noun marks its case directly and is not a member of the manqus class.
forbidden_answers: بَرِيءٌ يُعامل مثل القاضي لأنه ينتهي بحرف غير ثابت فيُحذف ويُستبدل بتنوين الكسر
بَرِيءٍ is correct because any noun that looks irregular at the end automatically belongs to the manqus class and drops its final letter the same way قاضٍ does.
required_reasoning: بَرِيءٌ is a hamza-final noun, not a member of the manqus/bare-glide-final class
the hamza bears its own case vowel and tanwin directly and visibly in every case
the manqus glide-drop rule applies only to a bare single glide preceded by kasra, and the hamza-final class does not qualify for it merely by resemblance
explanation: A post-long-vowel hamza marks its own case directly and visibly; extending the manqus glide-drop rule to it because both classes look irregular is a class-mismatch error.

concept: A masdar's own template realizes a weak radical independently of the finite verb's surface
prompt: The finite perfect قَالَ (root ق و ل) collapses its hollow middle radical و into the long vowel ا — a feature of the verb's own CāC template. A learner reasons that the masdar of this verb must show the identical alteration and derives it as قَال (copying the verb's own long-vowel surface). What is the correct masdar, and why doesn't it inherit the verb's alteration?
expected_answer: The correct masdar is قَوْل. A verbal noun's template is derived from the verb's own measure and realizes any weak radical in that template's own slots, never by copying the finite verb's own surface alteration. The masdar's CaCC-shaped template places the weak radical و in a stable vowelless slot immediately after a fatha (qa-w-l) — a completely different position from the finite perfect's own CāC template that collapses the same radical into a long vowel — so the masdar does not inherit the verb's own collapse.
accepted_variants: قَوْل is correct because the masdar's own template keeps the weak radical و as a plain vowelless consonant after a fatha, unlike the finite verb's collapsed long vowel.
forbidden_answers: المصدر يُكتب قَال لأن الفعل الماضي قَالَ يُكتب هكذا فيجب أن يتطابق معه المصدر
قَوْل is correct because a verbal noun is always spelled identically to its finite verb's own perfect-tense surface, since they share the same root.
required_reasoning: a verbal noun's template is derived from the verb's own measure, independently of the finite verb's own surface alteration
the masdar template places the weak radical و in a stable vowelless slot right after a fatha, a different position from the verb's own collapsed long vowel
the correct masdar is قَوْل, not a copy of the finite verb's own altered surface
explanation: A masdar's weak radical is realized in the masdar template's own slot, never copied unchanged from a finite verb's altered perfect-tense surface.

concept: Gemination check before assigning a final-glide noun to the manqus class
prompt: قَاضِ (root ق ض ي, a single bare glide after kasra) is manqus and drops that glide in the indefinite genitive, showing bare tanwin kasratan: قَاضِ. A learner sees عَدُوٌّ 'enemy' (root ع د و, whose last two radicals are the identical و-و merged under a shadda) 'also ends in a glide' and classifies it as manqus too, writing its indefinite genitive as عَدِ. Is this correct?
expected_answer: No. عَدُوٌّ's final glide is geminated — two identical radicals و-و merged under a shadda — not a single bare radical standing alone, so it does not qualify for the manqus class at all. It declines as an ordinary sound-final noun: the indefinite genitive is عَدُوٍّ, with a full visible vowel and tanwin on the geminated letter, never the dropped-glide/bare-tanwin form عَدِ that only a true single-bare-glide manqus noun like قَاضِ takes. Gemination must be checked before a final glide is assigned to the manqus class.
accepted_variants: عَدُوٍّ is correct because its final glide is a geminated pair of radicals, not a single bare glide, so it declines as an ordinary sound noun with full visible tanwin.
forbidden_answers: عَدُوٌّ منقوص مثل قاضٍ لأنه ينتهي بواو فيُحذف ويُستبدل بالتنوين
عَدُوٍّ is correct because any noun ending in a wāw automatically belongs to the manqus class the same way a noun ending in a bare yāʾ does.
required_reasoning: the final glide of عَدُوٌّ is geminated (two identical radicals merged under a shadda), not a single bare radical
a geminated final glide does not qualify for the manqus class and declines as an ordinary sound-final noun
gemination must be checked before classifying a final glide as manqus
explanation: A geminated final glide is two merged radicals, not the single bare radical the manqus class requires; the noun declines as an ordinary sound-final noun instead.

concept: The manqus glide-drop rule applies only to the indefinite nominative and genitive
prompt: A learner is asked for the indefinite nominative of the manqus noun قَاضِ 'judge' (root ق ض ي, a single bare glide ي preceded by kasra) and writes قَاضِيٌ — keeping the glide and adding damma plus tanwin, the way an ordinary sound noun would. What is actually correct, and in which case-slots does the glide survive?
expected_answer: The correct indefinite nominative is قَاضِ, not قَاضِيٌ. A manqus noun (single bare glide preceded by kasra) drops that glide in exactly the indefinite nominative and indefinite genitive, and tanwin kasratan alone stands in its place; the glide is written only in the indefinite accusative (قَاضِيًا) and throughout the definite forms (الْقَاضِي). Keeping the glide with a damma-tanwin in the nominative wrongly treats قَاضِ as an ordinary sound noun.
accepted_variants: قَاضِ, with the glide dropped and bare tanwin kasratan, is correct for the indefinite nominative; the glide only survives in the indefinite accusative and the definite forms.
forbidden_answers: قَاضِيٌ في حالة الرفع لأن الاسم يحتفظ بحرفه الأخير دائمًا مهما كانت الحالة الإعرابية
قَاضِ is correct because a manqus noun always drops its final glide in every one of the three cases, not just the indefinite nominative and genitive.
required_reasoning: a manqus noun (single bare glide preceded by kasra) drops that glide in the indefinite nominative and genitive
tanwin kasratan alone stands in the dropped glide's place in those two slots
the glide survives only in the indefinite accusative and throughout the definite forms
explanation: The manqus glide-drop rule is restricted to exactly two slots (indefinite nominative and genitive); the glide is retained everywhere else.

concept: Definiteness-agreement test distinguishing an attribute from a circumstantial
prompt: In رَأَيْتُ الرَّجُلَ الْقَادِمَ ('I saw the arriving man'), a learner sees that الْقَادِمَ is accusative and participle-shaped and labels it a circumstantial (hal), reasoning 'accusative participles are hal.' Is this correct? Run the definiteness-agreement test.
expected_answer: No. الْقَادِمَ is definite (it carries the definite article) and agrees with its head الرَّجُلَ in both definiteness and case — that agreement pattern is exactly what marks an ordinary attribute (na't), not a circumstantial. A circumstantial (hal) is always indefinite and accusative regardless of its head's own case or definiteness; because الْقَادِمَ is definite, it fails the hal test outright and must be labelled an attribute instead. Being accusative and participle-shaped is not sufficient by itself; the definiteness-agreement test decides the label.
accepted_variants: الْقَادِمَ is an ordinary attribute, not a hal, because it agrees with its definite head in both definiteness and case, which a true hal never does.
forbidden_answers: القادمَ حال لأنه منصوب وعلى صيغة اسم الفاعل بصرف النظر عن التعريف
الْقَادِمَ is correct as an ordinary attribute because a participle-shaped word can never function as a circumstantial (hal) in Arabic under any circumstances.
required_reasoning: الْقَادِمَ is definite and agrees with its head in both definiteness and case, which marks it an ordinary attribute
a circumstantial (hal) is always indefinite and accusative regardless of its head's own case or definiteness
the definiteness-agreement test, not accusative case alone, decides between attribute and circumstantial
explanation: Accusative case and participle shape alone do not license a hal reading; a modifier that agrees with its head in definiteness and case is an ordinary attribute instead.

concept: The promoted argument of a passive verb takes case from its new subject position
prompt: The active sentence كَتَبَ الطَّالِبُ الدَّرْسَ has الدَّرْسَ as its accusative direct object. A learner converts it to the passive and writes كُتِبَ الدَّرْسَ — keeping الدرس accusative because 'it's still the same word doing the same job.' What is the correct passive form, and why does the case change?
expected_answer: The correct passive is كُتِبَ الدَّرْسُ, with الدَّرْسُ marked nominative. When a verb is put into the passive, its original direct object is promoted to fill the subject slot (nā'ib al-fā'il) and takes its case from that new syntactic position — nominative — not the accusative it carried as an object before promotion. Case follows the word's syntactic position after the rewrite, not the position it held before it.
accepted_variants: الدَّرْسُ is correctly nominative in the passive because the promoted object now occupies the subject slot and is cased from that new position.
forbidden_answers: الدَّرْسَ يبقى منصوبًا في صيغة المبني للمجهول لأنه نفس الكلمة التي كانت مفعولًا به
الدَّرْسُ is correct as nominative because passive verbs in Arabic simply always happen to take a nominative noun right after them, regardless of what role that noun plays.
required_reasoning: the direct object is promoted to fill the subject slot (nā'ib al-fā'il) when the verb becomes passive
the promoted noun takes its case from its new syntactic position, which is nominative
case follows the position after the rewrite, not the accusative position it held before promotion
explanation: A promoted na'ib al-fa'il is cased from its new subject position, never left in the accusative it held as an object before the verb was made passive.

concept: A construct's second term is genitive independently of the first term's own case
prompt: In رَأَيْتُ كِتَابَ الطَّالِبِ ('I saw the student's book'), كِتَابَ is accusative because it is the object of رأيت. A learner reasons that since the first term of the construct is accusative, the second term must also be accusative, and writes الطَّالِبَ. Is this correct?
expected_answer: No. The second term of a construct (idafa) is genitive by virtue of the construct relation itself, independently of whatever case the first (head) term carries from its own governor; the head's case never propagates to the second term. So the correct form is رَأَيْتُ كِتَابَ الطَّالِبِ, with الطَّالِبِ staying genitive regardless of كِتَابَ's own accusative case.
accepted_variants: الطَّالِبِ stays genitive because a construct's second term is cased from the construct relation itself, never inherited from the first term's own governor-assigned case.
forbidden_answers: الطالبَ منصوب لأن المضاف منصوب أيضًا فيتبع الاسم الثاني حالة الاسم الأول
الطَّالِبِ is correct as genitive because it simply happens to come second in the sentence, and the second word in any two-word sequence is always genitive in Arabic.
required_reasoning: the second term of a construct is genitive by virtue of the construct relation itself
the case of the first (head) term never propagates to the second term
كِتَابَ is accusative from its own governor (the verb), independently of الطَّالِبِ's genitive case
explanation: A construct's second term is always genitive from the construct relation, regardless of the case the first term carries from its own separate governor.

concept: Grounding a category in its own Arabic licensing conditions rather than an English category
prompt: In يَذْهَبُ الطُّلَّابُ إِلَى الْمَدْرَسَةِ ('the students go to school'), the verb يَذْهَبُ comes first. A learner, mapping the Arabic fa'il onto the English category 'subject' — which normally precedes the verb in English — concludes that 'this sentence has no subject, or the subject must be missing,' because nothing precedes the verb. What's wrong with this reasoning?
expected_answer: This is wrong. الطُّلَّابُ is the fa'il (agent) of يَذْهَبُ, identified by its case (nominative) and its agreement relationship with the verb, not by its position relative to the verb; Arabic freely allows a verb-initial order in which the fa'il follows the verb. Mapping fa'il onto the English category 'subject' silently imports the English expectation that a subject must precede its verb, which is not how Arabic licenses or identifies this category at all — several Arabic categories have no true English counterpart, and importing an English category's positional assumption distorts the actual licensing conditions.
accepted_variants: الطُّلَّابُ is the fa'il here, found by its nominative case and agreement with the verb, not by whether it precedes or follows يَذْهَبُ; verb-initial order is ordinary in Arabic.
forbidden_answers: لا يوجد فاعل في الجملة لأن الفعل جاء أولاً والفاعل في الإنجليزية يسبق الفعل دائمًا
الطُّلَّابُ is correct as the fa'il only because it happens to sit right after the verb, since whatever noun immediately follows a verb in Arabic is automatically the fa'il.
required_reasoning: the fa'il is identified by its case and agreement with the verb, not by its position relative to the verb
Arabic freely allows verb-initial order, in which the fa'il follows the verb
mapping fa'il onto the English category 'subject' imports a positional assumption that does not hold for Arabic and distorts the licensing conditions
explanation: An Arabic category is learned from its own Arabic licensing environment (case and agreement here), never by importing an English category's positional assumptions.

concept: A governing masdar's agent is genitive as the idafa's second term, never nominative
prompt: In the phrase إِعْطَاءُ الْمُعَلِّمِ الْجَائِزَةَ ('the teacher's giving the prize'), a learner reasons that المعلم is the one performing the giving, so — just like a verb's subject — it should be nominative, and writes إِعْطَاءُ الْمُعَلِّمُ الْجَائِزَةَ. Is this correct?
expected_answer: No. A governing verbal noun's (masdar's) logical agent surfaces as the second term of an idafa built on the masdar, so it is genitive — الْمُعَلِّمِ — never nominative; marking it nominative wrongly treats it as if it were a finite verb's own subject. The correct phrase is إِعْطَاءُ الْمُعَلِّمِ الْجَائِزَةَ, with الْمُعَلِّمِ genitive as the masdar's agent term and الْجَائِزَةَ accusative as its object.
accepted_variants: الْمُعَلِّمِ is genitive because a governing masdar's logical agent fills the second-term idafa slot, unlike a finite verb's nominative subject.
forbidden_answers: المعلمُ فاعل حقيقي يقوم بالفعل فيُرفع مثل فاعل الفعل العادي
الْمُعَلِّمِ is correct as genitive only because every logical agent of any Arabic construction is automatically genitive, whether or not a governing verbal noun is actually involved.
required_reasoning: a governing masdar's logical agent surfaces as the second term of an idafa built on the masdar
that agent term is genitive, never nominative, because marking it nominative would wrongly treat it as a verb's own subject
الْمُعَلِّمِ is genitive here, distinct from الْجَائِزَةَ, which is accusative as the masdar's object
explanation: A masdar's own logical agent is genitive as its idafa second term; nominative marking would wrongly import a finite verb's subject case onto it.

concept: Recovering a forgotten grammatical label by decomposing its own ordinary components
prompt: A learner has forgotten what the term اسم الفاعل names and starts hunting for an external reference table to look it up, rather than working from the term itself. Show how decomposing the label's own ordinary Arabic components recovers its function faster, and state what اسم الفاعل means.
expected_answer: اسم الفاعل decomposes into اسم ('noun') and الفاعل ('the doer/agent'), so the label itself literally means 'the doer-noun' — the noun form that names whoever performs the action (e.g. كَاتِب 'writer' from كَتَبَ 'to write'). A memorized grammatical label is not an opaque code to be looked up separately; decomposing it into its own ordinary Arabic components recovers the category's function directly and faster than a lookup table, precisely because the terminology is motivated rather than arbitrary.
accepted_variants: اسم الفاعل means 'the doer-noun,' recoverable directly from its own two ordinary Arabic components without any separate lookup table.
forbidden_answers: لا يمكن معرفة معنى اسم الفاعل إلا بالرجوع إلى جدول مرجعي خارجي لأن المصطلح رمز مغلق
اسم الفاعل means 'the doer-noun' correct only because that is simply how every textbook glossary happens to translate it, not because the label's own components can be decomposed.
required_reasoning: اسم الفاعل decomposes into اسم ('noun') and الفاعل ('the doer/agent'), literally 'the doer-noun'
a memorized label is not an opaque code; decomposing it into its own ordinary components recovers its function
this decomposition route is faster than a separate lookup table because the terminology is motivated, not arbitrary
explanation: A forgotten grammatical label is recovered fastest by decomposing its own ordinary Arabic components, not by treating it as an opaque code requiring external lookup.

concept: Reserving the participle for identity/state readings, not narrated past events
prompt: A learner wants to say 'the student wrote the letter yesterday' and produces الطَّالِبُ كَاتِبٌ الرِّسَالَةَ أَمْسِ, using the active participle كَاتِبٌ to narrate the one-time completed writing. What's wrong, and what should be used instead?
expected_answer: This is wrong. An active participle names an identity, role, or persisting state of its referent (e.g. كَاتِبٌ 'a writer, one who writes' as an ongoing role), never a single bounded past occurrence; describing a specific, completed past event requires the perfect (finite) verb instead. The correct sentence is كَتَبَ الطَّالِبُ الرِّسَالَةَ أَمْسِ, using the perfect verb كَتَبَ to assert the one-time completed writing yesterday.
accepted_variants: كَتَبَ الطَّالِبُ الرِّسَالَةَ أَمْسِ is correct because a single completed past event needs the perfect verb, while the participle كَاتِبٌ only names an identity or ongoing role.
forbidden_answers: كَاتِبٌ يصلح لوصف حدث الأمس المكتمل لأنه من نفس الجذر ويحمل نفس المعنى تقريبًا
كَتَبَ الطَّالِبُ الرِّسَالَةَ أَمْسِ is correct only because the active participle form is grammatically forbidden in Arabic and could never be used in any sentence at all.
required_reasoning: an active participle names an identity, role, or persisting state, never a single bounded past occurrence
narrating a specific, completed past event requires the perfect (finite) verb
the correct sentence uses كَتَبَ, the perfect verb, not the participle كَاتِبٌ
explanation: A participle asserts identity or persisting state, not a single bounded occurrence; narrating a completed past event always requires the perfect verb.

concept: A governing masdar's object stays accusative under parent-verb government
prompt: In مُشَاهَدَةُ الطِّفْلِ الْفِيلْمَ ('the child's watching the film'), a learner reasons that a governing verbal noun 'chains' its arguments the way an idafa chains genitives, and marks الفيلم genitive too: مُشَاهَدَةُ الطِّفْلِ الْفِيلْمِ. Is this correct?
expected_answer: No. A verbal noun (masdar) that governs keeps the accusative on its object — exactly as its parent verb would — unless a preposition is used instead; the object is not folded into the idafa chain as a further genitive term. So الْفِيلْمَ stays accusative: مُشَاهَدَةُ الطِّفْلِ الْفِيلْمَ, with الطِّفْلِ genitive as the masdar's agent (the one idafa term) and الْفِيلْمَ accusative as its object under parent-verb government.
accepted_variants: الْفِيلْمَ stays accusative because the masdar governs its object exactly as its parent verb would, rather than chaining it into the idafa as a further genitive.
forbidden_answers: الفيلمِ مجرور لأن المصدر يُلحق كل معمولاته بصيغة الإضافة المتتالية
الْفِيلْمَ is correct as accusative only because the masdar's object happens to be definite here; if it were indefinite it would be chained into the idafa as a further genitive term instead.
required_reasoning: a governing masdar's object is marked accusative, exactly as its parent verb would govern it
the object is not folded into the idafa chain as a further genitive term
only the masdar's agent is the genitive idafa term; the object stays accusative
explanation: A governing masdar's object keeps the accusative its parent verb would assign; only the agent occupies the genitive idafa slot.

concept: Excluding a nominal template's own consonant from the root before counting radicals
prompt: مِفْتَاحٌ 'key' is an instrument noun (ism al-ala) built from the root ف ت ح 'to open' on the template مِفْعَال. A learner counts the initial م as a root letter and states the root is م ف ت ح (four letters). What's wrong, and what is the actual root?
expected_answer: This is wrong. The initial م of مِفْتَاحٌ is the instrument-noun template's own fixed consonant (the مِفْعَال pattern), not a root letter merely because it sits at the front of the word; excluding it by matching the whole surface against the closed template inventory leaves the genuine triliteral root ف ت ح. Counting the template's own مِـ as a radical produces a spurious four-letter root that does not actually exist.
accepted_variants: The root is ف ت ح; the initial م belongs to the مِفْعَال instrument-noun template and is excluded before radicals are counted.
forbidden_answers: جذر مِفْتَاحٍ هو م ف ت ح لأن الميم أول حرف في الكلمة فيُعدّ جزءًا من الجذر
The root ف ت ح is correct only because instrument nouns happen to have no fixed template at all, so every letter that appears in مِفْتَاحٌ is automatically part of the root by default.
required_reasoning: the initial م of مِفْتَاحٌ is the instrument-noun template's own fixed consonant, not a root letter
a template's own consonant is excluded from the root by matching the whole surface against the closed template inventory
the genuine root is the triliteral ف ت ح, not the spurious four-letter م ف ت ح
explanation: A nominal template's own fixed consonant is excluded from the root by checking the closed template inventory, never counted merely because it is adjacent to the radicals.

concept: The passive construction's defining agent absence forbids any agent-naming phrase
prompt: A learner wants to say 'the lesson was written by the student' and, modeling English, produces كُتِبَ الدَّرْسُ بِوَاسِطَةِ الطَّالِبِ — attaching an agent-naming phrase to the passive verb. What's wrong, and what should be done instead if the agent must be named?
expected_answer: This is wrong. The nā'ib al-fā'il construction (the passive) is defined by the agent's absence, so no agent-naming phrase — modelled on an English by-phrase or otherwise — may be attached to it. If the agent genuinely must be named, the fix is to switch to an active clause instead, never to bolt an agent phrase onto the passive: كَتَبَ الطَّالِبُ الدَّرْسَ ('the student wrote the lesson').
accepted_variants: An agent-naming phrase cannot be attached to the passive; if the agent must be named, the sentence must switch to the active clause كَتَبَ الطَّالِبُ الدَّرْسَ instead.
forbidden_answers: كُتِبَ الدَّرْسُ بِوَاسِطَةِ الطَّالِبِ صحيح لأنه يقابل صياغة الإنجليزية by مباشرة
The agent cannot be named here only because Arabic passive verbs happen to be incapable of taking any prepositional phrase at all, agent-naming or otherwise.
required_reasoning: the passive (nā'ib al-fā'il) construction is defined by the agent's absence
no agent-naming phrase, modelled on an English by-phrase or otherwise, may be attached to a passive verb
if the agent must genuinely be named, the fix is to switch to an active clause instead
explanation: The passive is defined by omitting the agent, so no agent-naming phrase is ever licensed on it; naming the agent requires switching to an active clause.

concept: Telling agent and patient participles of one root apart by template, not shared radicals
prompt: From the root ك ت ب, كَاتِبٌ (fa'il template) and مَكْتُوبٌ (maf'ul template) are built. A learner, noticing they share the same three radicals, translates مَكْتُوبٌ as 'the writer' and كَاتِبٌ as 'the written thing' — reading the shared radicals rather than the templates. What's wrong?
expected_answer: This reverses the two roles. كَاتِبٌ and مَكْتُوبٌ share the root ك ت ب but are told apart by their own prefix and internal vowel skeleton, not by their shared radicals: كَاتِبٌ (fa'il template) is the agent — 'writer, one who writes' — and مَكْتُوبٌ (maf'ul template) is the patient — 'written thing, that which is written.' Reading the shared radicals while ignoring which template is actually present reverses who acted and what was acted upon; the templates, not the root, assign the argument roles.
accepted_variants: كَاتِبٌ is the agent ('writer') and مَكْتُوبٌ is the patient ('written thing'); the fa'il/maf'ul templates, not the shared root letters, decide which role each form names.
forbidden_answers: كَاتِبٌ ومَكْتُوبٌ يحملان نفس المعنى تقريبًا لأنهما من نفس الجذر فيمكن استبدال أحدهما بالآخر

كَاتِبٌ is the agent and مَكْتُوبٌ is the patient correct only because كَاتِبٌ happens to be the first of the two words mentioned, and the first-mentioned word in any root-sharing pair is always the agent.
required_reasoning: كَاتِبٌ and مَكْتُوبٌ are told apart by their own prefix and vowel skeleton, not by their shared radicals
كَاتِبٌ (fa'il template) is the agent -- the doer -- and مَكْتُوبٌ (maf'ul template) is the patient -- the done-to
reading the shared radicals while ignoring the template reverses who acted and what was acted upon
explanation: Two derivatives of one root on different templates are distinguished by their own prefix/vowel skeleton; the shared radicals alone assign no argument role.

concept: Selecting the derivational form from the intended event, not from availability
prompt: A learner has just learned the active participle غَافِرٌ ('one who forgives') and, wanting to say 'the teacher forgave the student's mistake' (a single, completed act), reaches for the form that is freshly available and writes الْمُعَلِّمُ غَافِرٌ خَطَأَ الطَّالِبِ. What's wrong, and how should the derivational form be chosen here?
expected_answer: This is wrong. غَافِرٌ asserts a role or persisting state ('one who forgives, a forgiver') rather than one bounded occurrence, so it does not express 'forgave [once].' The derivational form must be selected from the event actually intended, not from whichever form is simplest or most recently learned; since a single completed act of forgiving is meant, the perfect verb is required: غَفَرَ الْمُعَلِّمُ خَطَأَ الطَّالِبِ.
accepted_variants: غَفَرَ الْمُعَلِّمُ خَطَأَ الطَّالِبِ is correct because a single completed act of forgiving needs the perfect verb; the participle غَافِرٌ only names an ongoing role, not the one-time act.
forbidden_answers: غَافِرٌ يكفي للتعبير عن أنه سامح الطالبَ مرة واحدة لأنه الشكل المتاح والمتعلم حديثًا
غَفَرَ الْمُعَلِّمُ خَطَأَ الطَّالِبِ is correct only because the active participle form غَافِرٌ happens to be grammatically banned outright and could never appear in any Arabic sentence.
required_reasoning: غَافِرٌ asserts a role or persisting state, not one bounded occurrence
the derivational form must be selected from the event actually intended, not from whichever form is simplest or most available
a single completed act of forgiving requires the perfect verb غَفَرَ, not the participle
explanation: The derivational form is chosen from the meaning actually intended, never from which form the learner happens to have available or find simplest.

concept: Checking for a verb before choosing between the fa'il and mubtada' labels
prompt: جَاءَ الطَّالِبُ ('the student came') and الطَّالِبُ مُجْتَهِدٌ ('the student is diligent') both have الطالبُ as the first noun. A learner calls الطالبُ 'the subject' in both sentences, importing the single English grammatical category 'subject.' Why is this not adequate, and what should each be called?
expected_answer: In جَاءَ الطَّالِبُ, الطَّالِبُ is a fa'il (agent), licensed only because a verb (جَاءَ) is present, and it behaves by the verb's own agreement rules. In الطَّالِبُ مُجْتَهِدٌ, الطَّالِبُ is a mubtada' (topic), licensed only in a verbless nominal sentence, and it behaves by different agreement rules with its predicate. These are two distinct Arabic categories with different licensing environments and different downstream behavior; one English label ('the subject') covering both silently imports English agreement/case assumptions that do not hold for either Arabic category and erases the distinction the presence or absence of a verb makes.
accepted_variants: الطالبُ is a fa'il in جَاءَ الطَّالِبُ because a verb licenses it, and a mubtada' in الطَّالِبُ مُجْتَهِدٌ because no verb is present; one English label cannot cover both.
forbidden_answers: كلاهما فاعل نحوياً لأن المبتدأ يُعامل كفاعل الجملة الاسمية دون التحقق من وجود فعل

الطالبُ is a fa'il in the first sentence and a mubtada' in the second correct only because Arabic randomly assigns different labels to the same noun with no underlying rule, so the presence of a verb is irrelevant.
required_reasoning: fa'il is licensed only where a verb is present and follows the verb's own agreement rules
mubtada' is licensed only in a verbless nominal sentence and follows different agreement rules with its predicate
one English label such as 'the subject' must not cover both categories, since their licensers and behavior differ
explanation: fa'il and mubtada' are distinguished by checking for a verb first; one has no true English counterpart and covering both with 'subject' loses the distinction.

concept: The passive is signalled by one fixed vowel pairing, not any vowel change
prompt: A learner wants the passive perfect of كَتَبَ (root ك ت ب, 'he wrote') and, believing that changing the vowels 'in some way' is what signals the passive, writes كَتِبَ. Is this a valid passive form? What's the actual rule?
expected_answer: No, كَتِبَ is not a valid passive. Arabic passive voice is signalled entirely by a fixed vowel pairing on the stem — damma then kasra in the perfect — never by any other vowel combination and never by an added or substituted consonant. The correct passive perfect is كُتِبَ (damma on ك, kasra on ت); any other pairing, such as كَتِبَ (fatha-kasra) or كُتَبَ (damma-fatha), fails to encode the passive regardless of which consonants are present.
accepted_variants: كُتِبَ (damma-kasra) is the only valid passive perfect pairing; كَتِبَ and any other vowel combination fail to encode the passive.
forbidden_answers: كَتِبَ صيغة مبنية للمجهول صحيحة لأن الحركات تغيرت عن صيغة الفعل المعلوم
كُتِبَ is correct only because any change at all to a verb's vowels automatically signals the passive voice, regardless of which specific vowel pairing is used.
required_reasoning: the passive is signalled entirely by a fixed vowel pairing on the stem -- damma then kasra in the perfect
any other vowel combination fails to encode the passive, regardless of the consonants present
the correct passive perfect of كَتَبَ is كُتِبَ, not كَتِبَ or any other pairing
explanation: Passive voice is carried by one fixed vowel pairing, not by any change in the vowels; only damma-kasra in the perfect encodes it.

concept: One invariant nunation shape covers all three cases on an alif-final noun
prompt: مُصْطَفًى ('a chosen one', an alif-final/maqsura noun) is indefinite in three different sentences, one nominative, one accusative, one genitive. A learner writes its nunation differently in each — assuming the tanwin shape must match the case the way it does on a sound noun (damma-tanwin nominative, kasra-tanwin genitive, fatha-tanwin accusative). What's wrong?
expected_answer: This is wrong. An alif-final (maqsura) noun like مُصْطَفًى cannot carry any vowel on its final alif in any case, so its case stays covert (muqaddar) in all three slots, and its written nunation is one single invariant shape — never varying by case the way a sound noun's tanwin does. مُصْطَفًى is written identically whether it functions as subject, object, or after a preposition; the single shape is used and the case is read from context/position, not from a case-varying tanwin.
accepted_variants: مُصْطَفًى keeps one invariant nunation shape in every case, since an alif-final noun's case is covert and never marked by a case-varying tanwin.
forbidden_answers: تُكتب تنوين مُصْطَفًى بشكل مختلف حسب الحالة الإعرابية كما في الاسم الصحيح الآخر
مُصْطَفًى keeps one invariant nunation shape correct only because alif-final nouns happen to never be usable in an indefinite context at all, not because the alif itself cannot carry a case vowel.
required_reasoning: an alif-final (maqsura) noun cannot carry any vowel on its final alif in any case
its case therefore stays covert (muqaddar) in all three slots
its written nunation is one single invariant shape, never varying by case
explanation: An alif-final noun's case is covert in every slot, so its nunation shape stays invariant across nominative, accusative, and genitive.

concept: Final-weak participle nunation replaces the dropped weak letter, not full retained letter
prompt: سَاعِ ('one who strives', the active participle of سَعَى, root س ع ي) is a final-weak participle. A learner writes its indefinite nominative as سَاعِيٌ — keeping the weak letter ي and adding a full damma-tanwin, the way a sound-final participle would. What is actually correct, and why?
expected_answer: The correct indefinite nominative is سَاعِ, not سَاعِيٌ. This final-weak participle belongs to the manqus class (single bare glide preceded by kasra), so in the indefinite nominative and genitive the weak letter ي is dropped and tanwin kasratan replaces it — the nunation replaces the dropped letter in exactly those two slots. Writing the weak letter with a full damma-tanwin treats the participle as if it were sound-final, which it is not; the retained-letter, full-nunation form سَاعِيٌ is wrong.
accepted_variants: سَاعِ is correct because this final-weak participle drops its weak letter in the indefinite nominative and genitive, with tanwin kasratan replacing it instead of a full damma-tanwin on a retained letter.
forbidden_answers: ساعِ تُكتب سَاعِيٌ في حالة الرفع لأنها اسم فاعل صحيح الآخر يحتفظ بحرفه الأخير
سَاعِ is correct only because every active participle in Arabic drops its final letter in the indefinite regardless of whether that letter is weak or an ordinary sound consonant.
required_reasoning: سَاعِ is a final-weak (manqus) participle: a single bare glide ي preceded by kasra
the weak letter is dropped in the indefinite nominative and genitive, and tanwin kasratan replaces it
writing the retained weak letter with full nunation, as in سَاعِيٌ, wrongly treats the participle as sound-final
explanation: A final-weak participle drops its weak letter in the indefinite nominative and genitive, with tanwin kasratan standing in its place, exactly as any manqus noun does.

concept: An alif cannot bear a visible short vowel; an alif-final noun's case is covert
prompt: مَعْنًى ('a meaning') is an alif-final noun. In a nominative sentence, a learner tries to mark its case the way a sound noun would and writes a damma directly on the final alif (a diacritic mark placed on the ى/ا itself) to show it is nominative. What's wrong with this, and how is its case actually marked?
expected_answer: This is wrong; an alif -- whether written ى or ا -- cannot bear a short vowel at all, so no diacritic can be placed directly on it in any case. مَعْنًى's case is covert: the exponent (the case vowel) is simply not pronounced or written on the final letter in any of the three cases, which is exactly why this class is called covert (muqaddar). Leaving the form unmarked and reading its case from context is correct; writing a visible short vowel on the alif is impossible and incorrect.
accepted_variants: مَعْنًى is left with no vowel written on its final alif in every case, because that alif cannot bear a short vowel and the case is covert, read from context instead.
forbidden_answers: توضع الضمة مباشرة على الألف في مَعْنًى لتوضيح حالة الرفع مثل أي اسم صحيح الآخر
مَعْنًى is left unmarked correct only because Arabic simply never marks case on any indefinite noun at all, not because this particular alif is incapable of carrying a short vowel.
required_reasoning: an alif cannot bear a short vowel at all, in any case
the case exponent of an alif-final noun is covert (muqaddar) -- not pronounced or written on the final letter
the form is left unmarked on the alif and its case is read from context, never from a visible vowel drawn on the alif
explanation: An alif-final noun's case exponent is covert because the alif itself cannot bear a short vowel; no diacritic is ever drawn on it.
